title:
PROBABILITY,
(MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE EVENTS)
objective: LO: I can identify mutually exclusive events and use the addition rule.

content.text: Mutually exclusive events cannot happen at the same time. If one occurs, the other cannot occur. For example, rolling a 3 and rolling a 5 on one die.
Addition rule: If A and B are mutually exclusive, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B). No need to subtract an intersection because it is zero.

examples.expr: Rolling odd and rolling even are ME
P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) when ME
Getting a 3 and getting odd are ME
P(A or B) always = P(A) + P(B)

key_idea.title: Key idea
key_idea.text: Mutually exclusive events have no overlap: P(A and B) = 0. Use simple addition for P(A or B).
key_idea.caption: Only when A and B cannot both happen

modelled_examples.label: Example 1 – identifying ME events
modelled_examples.question: State whether rolling a 6 and rolling an odd number on a die are mutually exclusive.
steps: 6 is even, so it is not odd
modelled_examples.explanation: 6 and odd numbers share no outcomes.

modelled_examples.label: Example 2 – addition rule
modelled_examples.question: A bag has 3 red, 4 blue, 2 green, 1 yellow marble. Find P(red or green).
steps: Events are ME (a marble cannot be two colours)
modelled_examples.explanation: Since a marble is one colour only, add the probabilities.

modelled_examples.label: Example 3 – not mutually exclusive
modelled_examples.question: Are 'rolling greater than 3' and 'rolling even' mutually exclusive?
modelled_examples.answer: Not mutually exclusive (4 and 6 are in both)
modelled_examples.explanation: If they share any outcome, they are not mutually exclusive.

modelled_examples.label: Example 4 – exhaustive events
modelled_examples.question: A card is drawn. Find P(red or black).
steps: Red and black are ME (a card is one colour)
modelled_examples.explanation: When ME events cover all outcomes, they are also exhaustive.
